opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's really what motivated a lot of the work we did on Aya. The honest answer is that most existing multilingual instruction data was never designed around what people value in today's models. It was mostly repurposed.

If you look at what was available before, it fell into two buckets. The first was academic NLP datasets: classification, question answering, named entity recognition, wrapped in templates to look like instructions. That's useful for some capabilities, but it's not what people do with these models. Nobody opens a chat interface to do sentiment classification on a movie review. They want to brainstorm, write, get advice, ask open-ended questions, and have a natural back-and-forth.

The second bucket was translation. You take a high-quality English instruction dataset and machine-translate it into dozens of languages. That gets you coverage on paper, but you inherit two big problems. One is translationese: the text is stilted and unnatural, and models learn to sound like that. The other, which I think is more fundamental, is that you're importing an English-speaking, often very Western, view of what's worth asking. The questions, cultural references, and assumptions about what a helpful answer looks like all come from one context. A speaker of Yoruba or Bengali or Turkish may care about very different things, like local history, food, legal systems, or family norms, and a translated dataset just doesn't capture that.

There's also a big quality and coverage gap. For many languages, especially lower-resourced ones, there was essentially nothing: no human-written, open-ended, conversational data at all. Even where data existed, it was rarely checked by fluent speakers. So you'd get answers that were technically in the language but not something a native speaker would find natural or useful.

So what we kept coming back to was that if you want models that serve people across the world, you need people from those language communities defining what good looks like. That's why so much of our effort went into participatory data collection: thousands of fluent speakers writing and editing prompts and completions in their own languages, reflecting their own priorities. It's slower and messier, but it's the only way I know to close the gap between what's in the data and what people actually value.

r001.rationale: It contrasts narrow academic tasks such as classification and named entity recognition with the open-ended brainstorming, writing, advice, and back-and-forth people want from general-purpose models.

r002.rationale: It says existing data often lacks open-ended conversational examples, but does not state that it tends to elicit completions that are too short.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of what exists today wasn't really built with what people actually want out of these models in mind. If you look at the multilingual instruction datasets that were available even a couple of years ago, a huge fraction of them were derived from academic NLP benchmarks. So you have these templated tasks: classify the sentiment of this sentence, answer this reading comprehension question, translate this phrase. And those are fine for measuring a narrow slice of capability, but they bear very little resemblance to how someone in Lagos or Jakarta or São Paulo actually sits down and interacts with a model. People want to brainstorm, they want to write an email to their landlord, they want to understand a medical form, they want to be creative. And almost none of that was represented.

The second big gap is that a lot of so-called multilingual data is really just English data that's been machine translated. And that gets you coverage on paper, but it inherits all the cultural assumptions of the source. So you end up with a model that can speak Swahili but talks about Thanksgiving. The grammar might be passable, but the content doesn't reflect the lived experience, the idioms, the references, the things people in that language community actually care about. We saw this really clearly with Aya, where the data that native speakers contributed looked quite different from the translated data, both in topic distribution and in what made a response feel good.

And then the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is the long tail. The distribution of available instruction data is extraordinarily skewed toward maybe ten or fifteen languages. For the vast majority of the world's languages, there's essentially nothing, and the quality of what exists drops off a cliff. So you have this situation where the people who could benefit most from these tools, because they have the fewest alternatives, are precisely the ones the data serves worst.

So when I think about where it falls short, it's really three things at once: the tasks don't match real usage, the content is culturally hollowed out by translation, and the coverage is deeply unequal. And fixing that isn't purely a technical problem. It requires actually involving the communities whose languages you're trying to serve, which is slower and messier than scraping, but I don't think there's a shortcut.

r001.rationale: It contrasts narrow, templated benchmark tasks with real interactions such as brainstorming, writing, and creative work, conveying the mismatch with broader, open-ended model use.

r002.rationale: It does not state that existing multilingual instruction data tends to produce completions that are too short.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a gap between what we call multilingual instruction data and what it actually captures. A lot of it starts with English instructions and translates them into other languages. That can be useful, but it preserves the assumptions about what an English-speaking user would ask and what a good answer looks like.

What people value goes beyond getting a grammatically correct response. Does the model understand their context? Does it use an appropriate register? Can they ask a question in the way they naturally communicate, including mixing languages, and get something useful back?

And instruction data often gives you one answer to imitate. It doesn’t necessarily tell you which of two plausible answers someone would prefer, or why. So we need more direct participation from speakers of those languages, both in creating the questions and in judging the responses. Otherwise, we risk measuring how well a model reproduces translated examples rather than how well it serves the people using it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a gap between having data in a language and having data that reflects what people who speak that language actually want from a model. A lot of multilingual instruction data starts with English prompts and translates them. That’s useful, but it carries over the assumptions about what questions matter, what a good answer looks like, and how someone should communicate.

People value more than grammatical fluency. They want a model that understands their context, follows instructions reliably, and responds in a way that feels appropriate. Those preferences can vary across communities, even within the same language. If all your examples come from translation, you’re not really capturing that variation.

So I think we need to move beyond asking, ‘How many languages does this dataset cover?’ and ask, ‘Who contributed to it, and whose preferences are represented?’ That means involving people in creating and evaluating instructions in their own languages, rather than assuming that preferences collected in English will transfer everywhere.

r001.rationale: The response discusses translated prompts and underrepresented community preferences, but does not identify a mismatch between narrow-answer NLP benchmarks and the fluid, extended responses people value.
